big: Small-cap funds have gathered very large sums. Since 2024, fund houses publish how many days it would take to sell a quarter and half of the portfolio. That number shows how crowded the exit door is.

lines: My small-cap fund says 32 days to sell half its portfolio. Does that mean my redemption will take 32 days?
No, and that is the mix-up to clear first. Let us see what the number really measures.

h: One slow stock sets the clock
alt: Bars of days needed to sell half of each of six holdings in a fund
caps: Fund B holds six stocks. Each bar: days to sell half of that stock, at 10% of its daily trading (assumed).
Busy stocks clear within a week. Thin ones take weeks.
A pro-rata exit sells all six together, so the slowest stock sets the pace for the whole fund.
That makes 32 days for 50% and 16 days for 25%. This is the figure the stress test reports.

alt: Bars comparing days to sell 25% and 50% for a small fund and a fund four times larger
caps: Same six holdings, same market. Fund A has ₹2,000 crore. Fund B has four times as much.
Four times the money means four times the days: 16 to sell 25%, against 4.
And 32 days to sell 50%, against 8. As a fund grows, the exit gets slower.
More days means a harder exit in a sell-off. It is a risk signal, not a payout delay.

alt: Two bars showing a fund's mix of easy, medium and thin stocks before and after heavy redemptions
caps: A made-up fund: 60% easy-to-sell stocks, 25% medium, 15% thin.
Heavy redemptions arrive: 40% of the fund. The manager sells the easy stocks first.
Those who stay now hold 33% easy, 42% medium and 25% thin. The next exit is harder.
Early leavers got better prices. This is the risk a stress test warns about.

rows.name: After 40% leave, easy stocks sold first

q: A small-cap fund shows 24 days to liquidate 50% of its portfolio, selling in proportion at a steady pace. How many days does the same test show for 25%?
why: Same days for half the amount would mean the selling pace doubled, which the test does not assume.
Halving the amount does not square the time. At a fixed pace, time scales in direct proportion to what is sold.
At a steady pace the time is proportional: half the portion needs half the days, so 12 here.
Doubling is what you would see when selling more, not less. A smaller portion needs fewer days, not more.

q: A client's small-cap fund shows 32 days to sell half its portfolio. She fears her own redemption will take 32 days. What is accurate?
opts: Yes, every redemption waits until the fund has sold its holdings
No, it is a stress scenario for a mass exit, not a payout delay
No, the figure applies only to institutions, not to retail investors
Yes, but only for redemptions above ₹10 lakh in that fund
why: Redemptions are normally paid in the usual time from cash and liquid holdings. The 32 days is a test, not a queue.
The test asks how long selling half pro rata would take if many investors left together. It does not delay normal payouts.
The figure describes the portfolio, which every investor shares. It is not split by type of investor.
The stress test sets no such threshold. It measures how liquid the portfolio is, not the size of one redemption.

q: A client with ₹50 lakh wants 40% in two small-cap funds, both showing about 40 days to liquidate half. What is the most useful advice?
opts: Accept it, since 40 days for half is standard for small caps
Spread the 40% over four small-cap funds to shorten the days
Keep 40%, but choose the fund that shows the fewest days
Size the slice to what he can hold through a deep fall
why: No fixed standard exists. Long days flag exit risk on top of small-cap swings, so the size still needs a deliberate choice.
Four funds in the same bucket hold overlapping stocks and the same swings, so the total risk and total exit time stay much alike.
Fewer days is a better tie-breaker, but a 40% slice stays too big if a sharp fall would make him sell in a panic.
Liquidity and volatility both argue for size. The slice should match what he can sit through, then days break ties.

q: A small-cap fund meets heavy redemptions by selling its most liquid stocks first. What happens to the investors who stay?
opts: Their mix turns thinner, so a second exit is harder
They gain, since the manager keeps only the best stocks
Nothing changes, because every investor shares pro rata
They are repaid first, because they stayed with the fund
why: The easy stocks go first, leaving a more illiquid mix. Early leavers get out at better prices than those who stay.
Best here means easiest to sell, not highest quality. What remains can be weaker on liquidity and harder to exit.
Investors do share pro rata, but the portfolio itself changes: it is left with the harder-to-sell stocks.
Redemptions are paid to those who ask, not to those who stay. Staying earns no priority in payment.

pts: The stress test reports days to sell 25% and 50% of a fund's holdings. More days means a harder exit in a sell-off.
It is not a payout delay. The cost of a crowded exit falls on the investors who stay.
Size small-cap slices to what a client can hold through a deep fall, and use the days to compare funds.
